TIME: 0.25 minutes

PURPOSE OF THIS LESSON
This is Lesson 6 of 12 in the evidence-gathering sequence. In Lessons 1–5, learners built conceptual models of cell structure and specialisation using diagrams, text, and discussion. Lesson 6 is the first direct empirical encounter with real cells under a microscope. By examining onion epidermal cells — the same onion that the Grade 10 student in Nairobi was slicing when the anchoring phenomenon began — learners gather first-hand visual evidence of plant cell structures. The observation that there are NO chloroplasts in onion skin cells generates productive surprise, deepens understanding of cell specialisation, and plants a key question that will drive Lessons 7–8 (animal cells, specialised cells). This lesson transitions the unit from conceptual modelling to evidence-based model revision.

BEFORE CLASS
Read the build log and complete the local practical risk assessment. Confirm the iodine product, concentration, SDS and quantities: V2 does not specify them. Trial the slide, focusing and field-diameter measurement on the actual microscopes. Have Version 3 models from L5 available. This pilot is pedagogically Lesson 6; Lessons 4–5 are prerequisites even though they are not in the pilot package.

DO
Introduce the practical. Do not show the comparison illustration (slide 18) or reveal the chloroplast outcome until every pupil has recorded observations.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Source proposes no-goggles handling and improvised pharmacy-iodine dilution. Those are unresolved safety issues, not approved substitutes. Do not implement these source fallbacks without qualified school approval. Notify the teacher of any school-recorded restriction on stain handling; a water-only option requires local approval and may give lower contrast. This draft does not approve a chemical formulation.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0 minutes

DO
Read before class; keep slides 2 and 3 hidden and use Presenter View. Notes follow TIME, DO, SAY, WAIT TIME, LOOK FOR, IF…, WHY THIS WORKS, ANSWER KEY, SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU, TEACHER REFLECTION.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0 minutes

DO
Before pupils arrive, test each microscope and prepare an example slide. Measure field diameter for the low-power objective used and record it with the objective; prepare an individual result sheet. Confirm every group’s kit. Materials: Per group of 3–4: one onion and one microscope as in the visual example; glass slides and coverslips, forceps and mounted needle, approved iodine stain/dropper and water, paper towels, practical books, pencil, ruler and new-colour pen. Goggles and lab coats for each pupil. Shared: designated broken-glass container, board/timer, two note colours, transparent ruler for field calibration. Exact counts of reusable/consumable items and stain product/concentration must be confirmed by the teacher; do not infer a pharmacy formulation.

IF…
Too few microscopes: rotate groups as the source permits; keep group size 3–4 where possible. No microscope: a teacher may review a verified actual image/video route, clearly identified as secondary evidence; no such media is supplied or verified here. A comparison drawing is not a substitute for a claimed real observation. If the safe stain/PPE/calibration route is unresolved, the practical is not ready for classroom use.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Open safety items: no-goggles fallback, improvised iodine tincture dilution, product/concentration, disposal and any individual restrictions need the school’s approval. No chemical concentration is invented.

TIME: 0.5 minutes

DO
Point to Lesson 6. Link the prior plant/animal diagrams to today’s first onion observation. The pilot set is not the full taught sequence.

SAY
We have used drawings. Today we look at the onion from Amina’s story through a microscope. The practical builds on Lessons 4 and 5.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0.75 minutes

DO
Introduce goals without revealing whether chloroplasts will be visible. Explain vocabulary from prior lessons only.

SAY
We will prepare, observe and measure. Your own results matter more than matching a drawing.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 1.5 minutes

DO
Read each rule before materials are handled. Point to the glass/waste containers, PPE and spill instructions. Use mounted needles only as demonstrated. Confirm school-approved stain handling, disposal and individual restrictions; no source shortcut is approved here.

SAY
Stop and tell me if glass breaks or equipment is unsafe. Ask before using a material or changing the method.

LOOK FOR
Goggles/coats worn for staining, safe glass handling and clear cables; monitor continuously.

IF…
If the required equipment or risk controls are absent, stop the practical component and refer to the teacher’s approved plan. Do not treat arm’s-length work as eye protection.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
V2 includes unsafe/unvalidated substitution suggestions. They are retained as explicit review issues in hidden notes and the build log, not as student instructions. This deck is not a local risk assessment or a stain recipe.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

PREDICT PHASE (8 minutes total)
TIME: 6 minutes

DO
Hold up the whole onion. Give 4 minutes independent sketching/writing, then 2 minutes paired comparison. Pupils list expected structures and predict chloroplast presence with a reason.

SAY
Sketch one cell. Label the structures you expect. Will you see chloroplasts? Give a reason.

WAIT TIME
4 minutes silent work; 2 minutes partner talk.

LOOK FOR
Every pupil attempts at least three structures and a reasoned prediction. Note pupils needing vocabulary support.

IF…
If no structures are named, record the starting point and pair with a supportive peer during Observe; do not show the comparison diagram.

ANSWER KEY
No result is supplied before observing. Record the pupil’s prediction and reason, to be tested against their actual view.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Cold-call four pairs: one strong predictor, one predicting chloroplasts, one not predicting them and one unsure. Scribe their ideas without correction. Count hands predicting chloroplasts and save the count.

SAY
Name one structure you predicted and WHY. We will revisit the count after observing.

WAIT TIME
5–10 seconds after asking for a reason.

LOOK FOR
Predictions include reasons; the class count is recorded, not supplied.

IF…
If pupils request the right answer, say: Keep your idea. Record what the microscope shows before we decide.

ANSWER KEY
Individual predictions and class count vary; no expected result or invented count.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

OBSERVE PHASE (38 minutes total: demo 8, method 3, group work 27)
TIME: 8 minutes

DO
Demonstrate every step with a think-aloud: peel transparent inner epidermis, lay flat with forceps, use ONE drop of the locally approved iodine product, lower coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle, then focus at low power. Say why folds/air bubbles affect the view. Teacher tests focusing/clearance on the actual instrument; use fine focus after changing to higher power. Invite three observations only after 10 seconds of looking.

SAY
Watch the method first. When you use the microscope, record what you actually see.

WAIT TIME
10 seconds of looking after a clear view is available.

LOOK FOR
Pupils can describe flat tissue and angled coverslip placement before beginning.

IF…
If the view is poor, re-focus and check tissue/air bubbles; do not announce structures pupils cannot see.

ANSWER KEY
Correct procedural sequence as demonstrated; no actual observation is prescribed.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Correct the source wording: iodine adds contrast; nuclear detail is variable. This is not evidence of starch in an onion nucleus. No nucleus is guaranteed visible in each cell. Use the exact school-approved formulation; V2 provides no concentration.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 3 minutes

DO
Before class, measure the low-power field diameter using the source’s transparent-ruler method and confirm it works with this microscope. Give the measured value and the matching objective to pupils. During group work pupils count cells end-to-end along their LONG axes and calculate an estimate. Do not supply 4 mm as if it were measured on this equipment.

SAY
Use our measured field diameter at the same objective. Divide by the number of cell lengths across that field.

LOOK FOR
Field diameter belongs to the objective used; count is along the cell long axis, with units retained.

IF…
If the field cannot be calibrated, flag that measurement as not completed. Do not substitute the illustrative example for a result.

ANSWER KEY
Estimated cell length (mm) = field diameter (mm) ÷ number of cell lengths across it. Convert mm to μm by multiplying by 1000. Numerical answers depend on actual measurements.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
The source ruler method needs local confirmation. An estimate from cell counts is approximate. Do not confuse total optical magnification with drawing magnification.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 27 minutes

DO
Groups of 3–4 make a slide. Each pupil draws 3–4 cells at low power and one at higher power, adds only observed labels and records total optical magnification. They also record chloroplast visibility and estimate one cell’s length using their own measurements. Circulate every 3 minutes; check at least six books. With five minutes left, ask everyone to check drawing/measurement completeness. Cold-call two groups to describe something visible.

SAY
Draw only what your microscope shows. Record unclear or not seen honestly. Do not copy a reference drawing.

WAIT TIME
Protect observation time; pupils work independently in their own books even when sharing a microscope.

LOOK FOR
Two drawings, optical magnification under each, actual observations, cell-size working/units. Distinguish visible wall from the unresolvable separate membrane.

IF…
For poor focus, revisit the demonstration at that microscope. If the nucleus/cytoplasm/vacuole is not resolved, record unclear rather than add a textbook label. An absent observation caused by a poor view is not proof of absence.

ANSWER KEY
No universal specimen drawing or numerical answer. Assess the record against the pupil’s actual view. Normal inner onion epidermis does not show chloroplasts; keep this expected outcome private until observations are recorded. Cell membrane is not separately resolved from the wall in this preparation.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
V2 demands four labels but also says the membrane is too thin to see separately. Accept honest variable visibility; flag the fixed four-label expectation for teacher review. Biological drawing: clear single pencil lines, no shading, non-crossing ruled labels, title and actual optical magnification.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

EXPLAIN PHASE (15 minutes total)
TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Give 2 minutes individual annotation in a new colour: circle confirmed predictions and mark those the observation did not support. Return to the actual class chloroplast prediction count; ask how many reported seeing them.

SAY
Use your drawing and notes as evidence. Was the view clear enough to judge?

WAIT TIME
2 minutes silent comparison.

LOOK FOR
Pupils revise from their own evidence rather than from an expected answer.

IF…
If green structures are reported, check tissue choice, optics and what was actually seen. Do not erase an unusual report to force the class result.

ANSWER KEY
Revisions depend on the recorded view. Typical inner bulb epidermis lacks chloroplasts, but unclear imaging must not be treated as proof.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0.75 minutes

DO
Use this one question before moving to the next slide. Take three different pupils across the chain. Name specialisation only after pupils have reasoned through location, light and function.

SAY
Think about the inner layers of an onion bulb.

WAIT TIME
15 seconds after the first reasoning question; 5–10 seconds on the later questions.

LOOK FOR
A location/function explanation rather than merely they do not need them.

IF…
If pupils say only no need, ask: What does the structure do, and what is this tissue’s role?

ANSWER KEY
Inside the fleshy bulb layers; this tissue receives little light.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0.75 minutes

DO
Use this one question before moving to the next slide. Take three different pupils across the chain. Name specialisation only after pupils have reasoned through location, light and function.

SAY
Use the location of the sample to reason.

WAIT TIME
15 seconds after the first reasoning question; 5–10 seconds on the later questions.

LOOK FOR
A location/function explanation rather than merely they do not need them.

IF…
If pupils say only no need, ask: What does the structure do, and what is this tissue’s role?

ANSWER KEY
Inner bulb tissue receives little light; do not claim every onion bulb is entirely below ground.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0.75 minutes

DO
Use this one question before moving to the next slide. Take three different pupils across the chain. Name specialisation only after pupils have reasoned through location, light and function.

SAY
Connect their role with the sample’s location.

WAIT TIME
15 seconds after the first reasoning question; 5–10 seconds on the later questions.

LOOK FOR
A location/function explanation rather than merely they do not need them.

IF…
If pupils say only no need, ask: What does the structure do, and what is this tissue’s role?

ANSWER KEY
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis using light. Do not infer that all light-exposed plant cells must contain them.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 0.75 minutes

DO
Use this one question before moving to the next slide. Take three different pupils across the chain. Name specialisation only after pupils have reasoned through location, light and function.

SAY
How could the structure of a cell relate to its role?

WAIT TIME
15 seconds after the first reasoning question; 5–10 seconds on the later questions.

LOOK FOR
A location/function explanation rather than merely they do not need them.

IF…
If pupils say only no need, ask: What does the structure do, and what is this tissue’s role?

ANSWER KEY
The inner bulb epidermis is protective, non-photosynthetic tissue. The bulb’s fleshy tissues store reserves; do not assign all storage to the epidermis. This connects to cell specialisation.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 6 minutes

DO
Pupils write a Claim–Evidence–Reasoning explanation alone. Read four or five books while circulating. A connection to Amina’s finger can follow the three sentences.

SAY
What is your answer? What did your microscope show? How does the scientific idea link them?

WAIT TIME
6 minutes independent writing.

LOOK FOR
A claim, actual evidence and reasoning about photosynthesis/light/this cell type. Do not reward invented observations.

IF…
If the evidence is unclear, let the pupil state the limitation. For no need alone, use the source prompt: What does a chloroplast do? Where is this tissue?

ANSWER KEY
Source-grounded exemplar for a clear view: Inner onion bulb epidermal cells lack chloroplasts (claim). I did not observe chloroplasts in my prepared cells (evidence). Chloroplasts support photosynthesis, while this inner protective tissue is not a photosynthetic leaf tissue and receives little light (reasoning). The visual result supports this interpretation but an unclear view alone cannot establish absence.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Do not pre-fill pupil evidence. The healing link is the principle of different structures/roles, not a claim that this onion experiment directly observed wound-healing cell mechanisms.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Only now show the comparison illustration. Ask what matches and what was unclear. Pupils may note missed observations only if they can actually verify them; they must not replace their evidence with this drawing.

SAY
This is an illustration, not a photograph or a guaranteed view. Which features could you identify in your own preparation?

LOOK FOR
Wall versus interior, variable nucleus visibility, no fabricated membrane boundary or chloroplasts.

IF…
If pupils begin copying the drawing as their observation, return to the microscope record and label this as a reference only.

ANSWER KEY
Illustration: adjacent elongated cells with walls, thin peripheral cytoplasm, central vacuolar region and sometimes a visible nucleus. The separate plasma membrane is not resolved. Real cells, clarity and staining vary.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
A visible nucleus is not guaranteed in every cell or field. The large central region may be inferred as vacuole without a clearly resolved boundary. Never use this schematic as a claimed actual result.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 2 minutes

DO
Use the source’s numerical example only after pupils have measured. Compare method and units, not whether their result equals this example. Their field/cell count may differ.

SAY
These numbers illustrate the method; they are not our class measurements.

LOOK FOR
Field diameter divided by cell count, then correct mm-to-μm conversion.

IF…
If the pupil multiplies D by n, ask how many cell lengths share the field. If units are missing, return to the measurement headings.

ANSWER KEY
Illustrative source example: 4 mm ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33 mm. 0.33 mm × 1000 ≈ 330 μm. The answer is approximate and refers to the counted long axis. Do not call the low-power field 4 mm unless actually measured.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

DRIVING QUESTION BOARD PHASE (7 minutes total)
TIME: 7 minutes

DO
Each group gets two note colours. Give 3 minutes to write one evidence note and one genuine question; post them and read three or four notes. The class votes on whether each claim is supported by today’s evidence.

SAY
Use something YOUR microscope showed. Thumbs up: supported; sideways: partly; down: not sure yet.

WAIT TIME
3 minutes group writing; pause for reasons after each vote.

LOOK FOR
Every group’s evidence note refers to an actual observation and names its limits.

IF…
For textbook-only statements ask the source prompt: Can you rewrite this using something you actually saw today?

ANSWER KEY
Evidence and questions vary. A valid claim names an observation; it does not claim today’s onion view proves animal-cell features. A source/reference connection must be labelled as such.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

MODEL BUILDING PHASE (6 minutes total)
TIME: 6 minutes

DO
Use the Version 3 plant-cell model from Lesson 5, not a new replacement drawing. Give 5 minutes of revision/evidence caption. In the final minute pupils predict a specific animal-cell difference for Lesson 7; sample three responses briefly within the final minute. Collect one group’s books for feedback.

SAY
Separate a direct observation from a feature inferred using earlier diagrams. Cite your evidence source.

LOOK FOR
At least one new-colour evidence-based revision; accurate chloroplast wording; a specific next-lesson prediction.

IF…
If a pupil adds detail never seen, ask: Was this observed today, or learned from a diagram? Label the source honestly. Do not judge wall thickness from an uncalibrated sketch.

ANSWER KEY
Accept supported wall/shape/cytoplasm observations and uncertainty. Chloroplast note: many photosynthetic plant cells contain chloroplasts; the inner bulb epidermis sampled here does not normally show them; human cells do not have them. A possible prediction is that cheek cells will have no rigid cell wall; retain it as a prediction, not today’s observation.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU
Correct the source overgeneralisation that chloroplasts occur ONLY in cells exposed to light: cell type and development matter, and light exposure alone is not sufficient. Retain the cell-role link without saying cells deliberately choose organelles.
Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TIME: 3 minutes

DO
Pupils complete the L6 row with their actual observations, measurement and explanation. Link back to Amina’s onion and healing finger. Close with the Lesson 7 teaser.

SAY
What did we observe? What did we learn? How does this help us think about the phenomenon?

LOOK FOR
Evidence is not replaced by expected observations; size units and specimen limitations remain explicit.

IF…
If the phenomenon link is too strong, distinguish the broad structure/function principle from mechanisms not observed here.

ANSWER KEY
Observe: actual prepared onion-cell features, optical magnification and measured/estimated length, including unclear details. Learn: an inner bulb epidermal cell is not identical to a generalised photosynthetic plant-cell drawing; structure and function vary with tissue. Explain: this supports investigating different cell roles, like the developing explanation of Amina’s healing cut; the experiment does not directly demonstrate wound repair.

SCIENCE NOTE FOR YOU

Source: V2 Cell Structure, Lesson 6. Review draft: native PowerPoint, ARES and teacher sign-off remain unverified.

TEACHER REFLECTION
1. Did all pupils record two honest drawings and a size estimate?
2. Which visibility/focusing/calibration problems need follow-up?
3. Did CER responses distinguish evidence from an expected answer?
4. Were safety controls followed, and which build-log issues need resolution?
5. Do model revisions cite observations and preserve genuine questions?
